title: What is SEWA AI? The clinical intelligence platform explained
subtitle: A complete walkthrough of the platform, from DICOM ingestion to clinical report
excerpt: SEWA AI is a trust-first clinical imaging platform that triages and prioritises critical radiology findings. This post explains exactly how it works — from the moment a scan arrives to the moment a radiologist acts.
content:
The problem SEWA was built to solve

Every day, thousands of chest X-rays, CT head scans, CT chest scans, and CT angiograms arrive in NHS radiology departments with the same anxious question: is there something urgent here, and has anyone noticed it? The stakes could not be higher. An undetected intracranial haemorrhage, a missed pulmonary embolism, an unnoticed pneumothorax — each represents a window in which clinical intervention could have changed the outcome.

SEWA AI is a clinical imaging intelligence platform designed to triage and prioritise these time-critical findings, automatically flagging urgent studies and routing them to the top of the radiologist's worklist. But SEWA is not just another detection tool. It is a complete clinical intelligence platform — from DICOM ingestion through AI inference, uncertainty quantification, hallucination screening, human sign-off, and reporting — built around one architectural principle: knowing when you do not know is as important as knowing what you do.

How SEWA works: the end-to-end pipeline

SEWA's pipeline processes a clinical scan through a series of interconnected stages, each designed to address a distinct failure mode in clinical AI. The platform currently covers adult thoracic and acute radiology — chest X-ray, CT head, CT chest, and CTA — with a modular architecture that allows additional modalities to be added without redesigning the core safety layers.

Stage 1: DICOM ingestion and pre-processing

When a DICOM study arrives — whether from a PACS system, a local workstation, or a Go DICOM edge device — SEWA ingests the series, normalises the pixel data, and prepares it for inference. The pre-processing pipeline handles common artefacts, checks series completeness, and flags studies that do not meet the expected protocol. Every step is logged, creating an audit trail from the moment the scan enters the system.

Stage 2: AI inference with uncertainty decomposition

The inference engine runs the study through a family of deep-learning models trained on thoracic and acute radiology. Rather than returning a single confidence score, each model returns an uncertainty decomposition — separating aleatoric uncertainty (noise inherent in the image data) from epistemic uncertainty (the model's own knowledge limitations). This decomposition is the foundation of SEWA's entire safety architecture.

Stage 3: The Metacognition Gate

Before any finding is dispatched to a clinician, the Metacognition Engine checks the output against anatomical, physiological, and contextual constraints. If the model proposes a finding that is inconsistent with the patient's demographics, the imaging modality, or basic clinical logic — or if its uncertainty is too high to make a reliable recommendation — the finding is flagged for deeper review rather than dispatched. The engine catches 96.3% of hallucinations in internal testing (n=500).

Stage 4: Database-layer human sign-off

A SEWA finding never becomes an approved clinical result unless a consultant radiologist has explicitly accepted it at the database layer. There is no UI prompt the user can dismiss, no administrator override, and no bypass path. Human oversight is structural — enforced by the data model itself, not by a workflow setting.

Stage 5: Reporting and handoff

Once signed off, the finding — along with its uncertainty decomposition, hallucination-gate status, and sign-off record — is available in the reporting workflow. The platform generates structured findings that integrate with existing radiology information systems, ensuring that SEWA augments rather than replaces the clinical workflow.

What makes SEWA different

The differentiators are architectural, not cosmetic. Most clinical AI platforms offer a detection score and a notification. SEWA offers a complete trust stack: uncertainty quantification, a hallucination gate, non-bypassable sign-off, and offline continuity — each addressing a documented reason that NHS AI adoption stalls. The platform is UK-sovereign, zero-PHI-egress, and designed for both cloud and edge deployment.

SEWA is at Technology Readiness Level 5 (TRL 5), with internal engineering results including an AUC-ROC of 0.961 (n=14,200) and a catch rate of 96.3% (n=500). These are engineering tests, not clinical validation — and they are presented as such. The path to clinical evidence runs through a prospective shadow trial, an NIHR EME application, and ultimately UKCA Class IIb certification (planned Q2 2027).

A platform built for the NHS

SEWA was designed for the NHS environment from the ground up. It is listed on G-Cloud 14, meaning NHS Trusts can deploy it in under five business days without a competitive tender. It complies with NHS DSPT and GDPR requirements. It aligns with DCB0129 and DCB0160 governance standards. And it is built to work in environments where connectivity is unreliable — an edge deployment that runs on under 20 MB of RAM and syncs to the cloud when the network resumes.
